author: blu
body: fetch, post and resolve-dns were declared as operations of the Network effect in Foreword chapter Network and no handler for them existed anywhere, so the type checker vouched for the name and the build died at the end of emit with CDX2040. A name the compiler promises and cannot keep is worth less than no name. They are real here, and they are not in the foreword, for the reason that decides it: an implementation needs NetIO, NetIO is codex.os, and a foreword chapter may not depend on codex.os. A chapter that wants them cites this one.

author: blu
body: The declared rows were wrong as well as unimplemented. fetch was typed [Network.Read] -- but fetching sends a SYN and sends the request line, and net-io-connect says [Network.Read, Network.Write] because that is what it does. A read that writes to the wire is the laundering the effect system exists to refuse, and this quire is effect-exempt, so nothing would have caught it. All three operations declare both rows. The name says what it is for; the row says what it does.

author: blu
body: Scope is unaffected: lint-scoped-call keys on the callee's name, not on whether the name is a builtin, so fetch "https://host/x" is still checked against a Network.Read grant and still refused with CDX4002.

author: blu
body: The addresses codex-vm's user-mode NAT hands out. The gateway answers ARP and forwards; 10.0.2.3 is its DNS.

author: blu
body: Never write a character code down. Text is CCE inside and ASCII on the wire, and the two do not agree: in CCE the newline is 1 and the code 10 is the digit seven. Every code here is asked for.

author: blu
body: A URL is scheme://authority/path. The authority is host or host:port. The scheme is read, and it decides whether the request happens at all: https is refused, because this speaks HTTP and would otherwise fetch it in the clear. See The Refusal, below.

author: blu
body: An A-record query to the NAT's resolver over UDP. The destination MAC is the broadcast address because the ARP cache starts empty and the NAT answers for the gateway either way -- this is what NetworkStack's resolve-dst-mac already does for every TCP connection in the tree.

author: blu
body: HTTP/1.0 has two ways to end a body: the server names its length, or the server closes. Both are honoured. The length is the one that lets the read stop without waiting for a FIN, so it is checked first.

author: blu
body: A receive loop of our own rather than net-io-recv-raw, because that one returns only when a frame carried payload and so cannot see the FIN that ends a close-delimited body: it would spin out its whole budget after the last byte had already arrived. This one watches the connection state and stops on the close.

author: blu
body: The runtime chokepoint for the network authority scope, the twin of Fat16's fat16-scope-admits for the filesystem path. A program declaring [Network.Write "api.example.com"] has that authority written into its process-table cell by the boot grant (or copied in at spawn, or installed by the verified loader). The compile time checker only sees literal URLs; a URL built at runtime from input is exactly what this gate is here to catch, so the check reads the destination authority off the runtime url and compares it to the grant with the same relation the type checker uses: a host matches whole, a port is compared only when the grant names one, and an empty grant admits every host (an unscoped program is unrestricted, which is what the empty authority already means).

author: blu
body: net-request-authority mirrors the type checker's url-authority: it appends the scheme's default port when the url leaves it implicit, so a grant written "host:80" and a fetch of "http://host/" agree on the port the way they do at compile time.

author: blu
body: An https URL is not fetched by THIS function. It would be fetched in the CLEAR -- the cleartext path speaks HTTP/1.0 and negotiates nothing -- and a caller that wrote https has said, in the only way the URL lets them, that the bytes must not cross the wire unprotected. Honouring the scheme as a parse and ignoring it as a promise is how a transport-security bug gets shipped, so the request is refused.

author: blu
body: So the refusal is permanent by design rather than pending on somebody doing the work, and it names the function that does the job. A diagnostic that sends its reader looking for an unimplemented feature is worse than one that says nothing, because it looks like an answer.

author: blu
body: Two things enter from the caller and are never invented here, because a chapter that invents them invents a weak key or a lie: the client's ephemeral X25519 private key and 32-byte handshake random (entropy), and the trust anchors plus calendar time the server's certificate is checked against (the security policy). A caller with no anchors gets no authentication and this refuses to pretend otherwise.

author: blu
body: The bare one-argument `fetch` still refuses https below: it has nowhere to carry anchors or entropy, so it cannot make an authenticated connection, and an anonymous one under the https scheme would be exactly the false promise this project does not ship. Authenticated fetch is this function.

author: blu
body: One TLS record framed off the TCP byte stream. A record is a five-byte header whose last two bytes are the length of what follows, so the whole record is 5 + that. Bytes are pulled until a full record is present; a stream that stops before one completes ends the read rather than blocking forever.

author: blu
body: The bytes are pulled with a loop of this chapter's own rather than net-io-recv-raw, for the reason http-recv above gives about the cleartext path: net-io-recv-raw returns only when a frame carried payload, so it cannot tell a peer that has finished from a peer that is merely slow, and it spins out its whole fifty-million-iteration budget after the last byte has already arrived. The cleartext half was written that way from the start. This half was not, and nothing in the tree could show it: every loopback here keeps its connection open forever, so the spin never happened. The first foreign server this fetch ever met sent its response, sent a FIN, had the FIN acknowledged by the stack, and the client then sat for minutes with the entire body already in hand.

author: blu
body: An empty answer ends the read, and it means either the connection closed or the budget ran out. The caller does the same thing in both cases -- it stops -- so the two are not distinguished here; a field nobody reads is worth what no field is worth.

author: blu
body: The host out of the URL is what the certificate is checked against, in ASCII, because a certificate holds ASCII and `host` is CCE Text. This is the whole reason an https fetch can mean anything: the authority in the URL is the identity the caller asked for, so it is the identity the server has to prove. A certificate that is genuine but belongs to another host now fails the handshake instead of completing it.
